conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the clinic, which simply means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers like you.  

To help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’ll be using a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s just ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; the goal is simply to see where you are so we can best support you. Everything you share stays between us, and we can pause or stop at any point if you need a break.

We’ll take it one question at a time. When you’re ready, we can begin.  

First question: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has laughter felt hard to come by?

Oh… yeah, I’ve still been laughing. My husband made a goofy face while changing the baby’s diaper yesterday and it cracked me up. So, I guess I’d say I can laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby came, but the funny side of things is still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, I’ve definitely still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as often as before, but I can find the humor in things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to things—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or the walk we usually take around the neighborhood. They’re small, but they still feel nice to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
I wouldn’t say I blame myself really. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I might think “Did I eat something that upset her?” but the thought passes pretty quickly—I don’t dwell on it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I do get a little wave of worry, like when the baby’s sleeping longer than usual and I suddenly think, “Is she breathing okay?” It doesn’t last long, and once I check on her I’m fine, but yeah, those random anxious moments do pop up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had any real panic—just those quick “what-if” flashes when she’s super quiet or if I hear an odd noise on the baby monitor. It’s more a little jolt than an actual scared feeling, and it settles once I see she’s fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m keeping up fine—there’s the usual pile of laundry and the dishes, but it’s manageable. Once in a while, if she’s fussy and I haven’t slept much, I’ll think “Ugh, everything’s piling up,” but it passes once she naps or my husband takes over for a bit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—when the baby gives me a decent stretch, I’m out like a light. I don’t lie there feeling unhappy or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t say miserable—maybe just a little teary one evening when she wouldn’t latch and I was tired, but it lifted once she finally fed and dozed off. Most of the time I feel okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I teared up that one night with the latching trouble, but I haven’t had any big crying spells. Nothing feels overwhelming enough to make me cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’m tired sometimes, but I’ve never had any thoughts like that.

You've painted a picture of a mom who is navigating the normal ups and downs of new motherhood: still finding moments to laugh, enjoying her morning coffee, and taking neighborhood walks, while also describing the occasional fleeting worries when the baby is quiet or a brief sense of "everything piling up" on tired days. Your tears were limited to one tough feeding session, and you quickly felt better once your little one settled. Overall, you report no persistent low mood, guilt, sleep disruption from sadness, or thoughts of self-harm, and you continue to look forward to everyday pleasures.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>The mother describes specific, recurrent anxious thoughts about the baby's safety that arise without an external trigger, matching the description of occasional worry "sometimes" for no good reason.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to 0-3 severity; a total of 7 falls below the 8-point threshold indicating minimal likelihood of <med>postpartum depression</med>. Core symptoms of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>-such as pervasive anhedonia (<quote>still look forward to coffee and walks</quote>), persistent low mood (<quote>most of the time I feel okay</quote>), daily crying spells (<quote>no big crying spells</quote>), self-blame (<quote>thought passes quickly</quote>), insomnia secondary to mood (<quote>sleep pretty well</quote>), and self-harm ideation (<quote>never had any thoughts like that</quote>)-were all denied or rated at the lowest severity. Brief situational anxiety and a single tearful episode do not meet clinical thresholds. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum follow-up with your <med>obstetric provider</med> at your next scheduled visit
2. Practice healthy coping strategies: enlist partner support for breaks, maintain daily outdoor activity, and keep consistent sleep-when-baby-sleeps habits
3. Re-screen with EPDS at 2- and 6-month postpartum visits or sooner if mood, anxiety, or functioning deteriorates
4. Contact the office promptly if you notice persistent sadness, loss of interest, marked anxiety, or any thoughts of self-harm
5. Consider joining a local new-mother group or online forum for additional peer support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (date of screening: —)  
Responses to 10-item Edinburgh-based verbal screen:

Symptoms endorsed  
• Transient tearfulness (1 episode related to infant-feeding difficulty)  
• Occasional, brief “what-if” worries about infant safety; no persistent generalized anxiety  
• Mild, situational feeling of “everything piling up” when sleep-deprived; resolves with support

Symptoms denied  
• Persistent low mood, anhedonia, pervasive guilt/self-blame  
• Sleep disruption secondary to mood (sleeps when baby sleeps)  
• Panic episodes, crying spells, suicidal or self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Overall mood remains positive; enjoyment of small daily activities preserved. Anxiety symptoms are situational, short-lived, and without functional impairment. No evidence of major depressive or anxiety disorder on this screen.

Risk factors  
None of the high-risk indicators (persistent sadness, anhedonia, guilt, mood-related insomnia, self-harm thoughts) identified.

Screening impression  
No clinical red flags for postpartum depression or anxiety at present; routine surveillance and supportive education recommended.
